name: Ice Axe Self-Arrest
description: The foundational emergency technique to stop an uncontrolled slide down a snow or ice slope before hitting rocks, cliffs, or crevasses.
steps: Instantly call out 'Falling!' to alert rope team members to drop into arrest stance.
Roll onto your stomach facing the slope with head pointing uphill.
Plant the ice axe pick into the snow near your uphill shoulder with both hands on the shaft and adze/pick.
Drive weight onto the chest directly over the pick to forcefully bite into the hard snowpack.
Kick toes into the snow if wearing boots; KEEP CRAMPON POINTS OFF THE SNOW to prevent flipping backwards if crampons catch.
goldenRule: Execute within 0.5 seconds before falling velocity accelerates beyond human arrest threshold.

name: Crampon Techniques (French vs Front-Pointing)
description: Efficient footwork methods to conserve calf muscle energy while maintaining maximum traction on steep frozen surfaces.
steps: Piolet-Canne (Cane Position): Ice axe held in uphill hand used as walking stick on low-angle slopes (up to 30°).
French Technique (Flat-Footing / 10-Point): Flex ankles so all 10 base crampon points remain flat on snow/ice simultaneously on moderate slopes (30°-50°).
Piolet-Panne (Cross-Body): Ice axe adze pressed across the chest while traversing steep crust.
Front-Pointing (German Style): On vertical ice (>50°), drive the two horizontal or vertical front points directly into the ice with calves dropped level to minimize burn.
goldenRule: Walk with feet shoulder-width apart in a wide 'cowboy' stance to avoid snagging crampon points on pant cuffs.

name: Crevasse Rescue: 3:1 Z-Pulley Haul System
description: A mechanical advantage hauling system assembled using prusik cords, carabiners, and pulleys to hoist a fallen climber out of a glacial abyss.
steps: Arrest the initial fall and establish a bombproof snow picket or deadman anchor.
Transfer the fallen climber's load off your harness and onto the snow anchor using a friction hitch (Prusik / Machard).
Approach the crevasse lip with safety backup, pad the snow lip with an ice axe or backpack to prevent the rope from cutting deep trenches.
Attach a directional pulley to the anchor line and a hauling prusik onto the climber's rope strands.
Reeve the rope back through the hauling pulley creating a 3:1 mechanical advantage ('Z-Rig') requiring one-third the manual hauling effort.
goldenRule: Always pad the crevasse lip before hauling; unpadded ropes slice through firn ice like cheese wire, locking the haul system.

name: High-Altitude Snow & Ice Anchors
description: Constructing solid load-bearing anchor points in variable snow and alpine ice conditions.
steps: Ice Screws: Drive 16-22cm chromoly ice screws at a positive 100° angle into dense blue/green water ice.
Snow Pickets: Drive aluminum T-section pickets vertically at 70° relative to fall line in firm snow, or bury horizontally as a 'Deadman' anchor in soft firn.
T-Slot (Deadman): Bury a snow shovel, ice axe, or stuff sack filled with snow 50cm-1m deep, tied off with a clove hitch.
V-Thread (Abalakov): Bore two intersecting 22cm ice screw holes to form an ice tunnel for zero-hardware rappelling.
goldenRule: Test all snow anchors with progressive bodyweight bounces before committing full expedition load.
